summary:
Goa stands under India's national framework: the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019 and its March 2026 amendment operate in this state exactly as in every other state and union territory, and no Goan statute or enforcement pattern diverging from the national position is on file.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, with both houses approving it and the bill awaiting presidential assent. The amendment removes the self-identification route established by the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment in the National Legal Services Authority case, restricts legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, and makes medical certification mandatory, with medical-board and district-authority approval required before gender-affirming surgery.

Trans men, trans women and non-binary or gender-fluid people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme; critics warn that the narrower definition excludes them. The government presents the amendment as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe it as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. Passage was met with protests in Mumbai.

The amendment adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these provisions echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held to cover gender identity and sexual orientation; the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to employment. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults under the new code.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to undergo a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at a station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.

Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment was passed amid street protests in Mumbai, and the People's Union for Civil Liberties has framed its new offences as a return to the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. Civil-society opposition is organised and vocal, but the bill's provisions take effect on presidential assent, which the sources record as still pending.

State-level practice across India varies widely enough to shape what a visitor sees. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha maintain transgender welfare boards and publicly funded surgery, while other states provide benefits chiefly to hijras; Goa's own position within that spread is not recorded.

Official assessments of police conduct conflict. A foreign government policy note from December 2025 describes police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited and non-systemic, whereas documented victim interviews from June 2024 describe abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. Both descriptions concern the same national apparatus a visitor would encounter.

Protection machinery exists alongside persistent abuse: the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police mandate police sensitisation and ban conversion therapy, yet clandestine conversion-practice networks continue to operate despite that judgment and the National Medical Commission's 2022 ban.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill has received presidential assent is unresolved in the sources, which record it as awaiting assent at the time of passage on 25 March 2026.

No Goan statute, Goan court judgment, or Goa Police enforcement record concerning transgender people is on file, so the state-level picture beyond the national framework remains not sourced. Whether Goa operates a transgender welfare board, state pension, or public-hospital surgery provision comparable to Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra or Odisha is not sourced.

Whether the April 2024 Ayushman Bharat expansion covering transition-related healthcare is implemented and accessible in Goa is not sourced. Likewise, no Goan data on conversion-practice networks, on treatment of trans detainees, or on intersex surgery practices appears in the inventory.

The sources do not establish how often passport or airport medical checks are applied to transgender travellers generally, only that individual cases have been documented and challenged in court.
